quickTip: Check apical pulse for a full minute before each dose; hold if HR under 60 or SBP under 90 and notify the provider.
administration: Give tartrate (Lopressor) with or right after meals; succinate (Toprol-XL) once daily, swallowed whole. IV push slowly over 2-5 minutes with cardiac monitoring.
mechanism: Blocks beta-1 receptors in the heart so it beats slower and with less force, lowering blood pressure and oxygen demand.
simplified: Takes the heart's foot off the gas pedal.
nursing: Hold for HR under 60 or SBP under 90; assess apical pulse before every dose.
Never stop abruptly - taper over 1-2 weeks to avoid rebound tachycardia, angina, or MI.
Diabetics: masks tachycardia and tremor of hypoglycemia; sweating still occurs, so check glucose.
Teach to rise slowly and report shortness of breath, edema, or sudden weight gain.
Preferred over nonselective agents in asthma/COPD, but still use cautiously.

quickTip: Nonselective means it blocks beta-2 in the lungs too - contraindicated in asthma and COPD because it can trigger bronchospasm.
administration: Give consistently with food to improve absorption; extended-release once daily, do not crush. IV only for emergencies with continuous ECG.
mechanism: Blocks both beta-1 (heart) and beta-2 (lungs, vessels) receptors, slowing the heart and blunting the body's adrenaline response.
simplified: Mutes adrenaline everywhere - heart, lungs, and nerves.
nursing: Assess lung sounds and respiratory history; avoid in asthma, COPD, and heart block.
Hold for HR under 60 or SBP under 90 and notify the provider.
Taper gradually - abrupt withdrawal can cause rebound hypertension and angina.
Monitor diabetics closely; hypoglycemia warning signs are hidden except sweating.
Screen for mood changes; report new depression or vivid dreams.

quickTip: Dry hacking cough is the classic side effect; angioedema (facial or tongue swelling) is the emergency - stop the drug and call for help immediately.
administration: Once daily, with or without food. Give the first dose at bedtime to reduce first-dose hypotension.
mechanism: Stops the enzyme that turns angiotensin I into angiotensin II, so vessels relax and the body holds less sodium and water.
simplified: Cuts the wire that tells vessels to squeeze.
nursing: Monitor BP, potassium, BUN, and creatinine; hold and notify for K+ above 5.0.
Absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy - teach reliable contraception.
Avoid potassium supplements, salt substitutes, and NSAIDs.
Teach that a persistent dry cough is expected; swelling of lips or tongue is an emergency.
Rise slowly; first-dose hypotension is common, especially with diuretics.

quickTip: Same benefits and precautions as ACE inhibitors but without the cough - it is the go-to switch when a patient cannot tolerate lisinopril.
administration: Once daily with or without food; may be split into two doses if BP control is uneven.
mechanism: Blocks angiotensin II from binding to its receptors, so vessels cannot constrict and aldosterone release drops.
simplified: Plugs the keyhole so angiotensin cannot turn the lock.
nursing: Monitor BP, potassium, and renal function; hold for K+ above 5.0 or rising creatinine.
Contraindicated in pregnancy - stop as soon as pregnancy is detected.
Avoid salt substitutes containing potassium and routine NSAID use.
Full effect takes 3-6 weeks; do not adjust the dose early.
Angioedema is rare but possible even without prior ACE inhibitor reaction.

quickTip: Works mostly on blood vessels, not the heart, so expect ankle swelling and flushing rather than bradycardia.
administration: Once daily, any time of day, with or without food. Avoid grapefruit juice, which raises drug levels.
mechanism: Blocks calcium from entering smooth muscle in artery walls, so the vessels relax and blood pressure falls.
simplified: Loosens the belt around the arteries.
nursing: Check BP and pulse before giving; hold for SBP under 90.
Ankle edema is dose-related and not fluid overload; elevate legs and report if severe.
Teach to avoid grapefruit and to rise slowly from sitting.
Encourage good oral hygiene to limit gingival hyperplasia.
Long half-life - missed doses can be taken the same day but never doubled.

quickTip: Slows the heart as well as relaxing vessels, so hold for HR under 60 - and never combine with a beta blocker IV without a clear order.
administration: Extended-release capsules swallowed whole, do not crush or chew. IV bolus over 2 minutes, then continuous infusion with ECG monitoring.
mechanism: Blocks calcium channels in both the heart's conduction system and vessel walls, slowing AV conduction and dilating arteries.
simplified: Puts the brakes on the heart and loosens the pipes at once.
nursing: Assess HR, BP, and rhythm before dosing; hold for HR under 60 or SBP under 90.
Watch for AV block on the monitor, especially with digoxin or beta blockers.
Avoid grapefruit juice; teach to rise slowly.
Contraindicated in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.
Increase fluids and fiber to manage constipation.

quickTip: Narrow therapeutic range 0.5-2.0 ng/mL. Low potassium makes toxicity more likely; early toxicity looks like nausea, anorexia, and yellow-green halos.
administration: Take apical pulse for one full minute before each dose. Give at the same time daily; IV over at least 5 minutes.
mechanism: Inhibits the sodium-potassium pump in heart cells so more calcium stays inside, making each beat stronger while slowing conduction through the AV node.
simplified: Makes the heart squeeze harder but beat slower.
nursing: Hold for apical HR under 60 (adult), under 70 (child), or under 90-110 (infant) and notify.
Monitor digoxin level, potassium, magnesium, and renal function; hypokalemia raises toxicity risk.
Antidote for severe toxicity is digoxin immune Fab (Digibind/DigiFab).
Teach to report anorexia, nausea, or visual halos - these appear before dangerous rhythms.
Loop and thiazide diuretics lower potassium; older adults need lower doses.

quickTip: Sublingual: one tablet every 5 minutes, up to 3 doses. Call 911 if pain is not relieved after the first dose. Never with sildenafil or similar drugs.
administration: Sublingual tablet dissolved under the tongue, not swallowed; sit down first. Patch on hairless skin, rotated daily with a 10-12 hour nitrate-free interval. IV via glass bottle and non-PVC tubing, titrated to BP.
mechanism: Converts to nitric oxide, which relaxes vein and artery walls, lowering the heart's workload and opening coronary vessels.
simplified: Opens the pipes so the heart works less.
nursing: Check BP before and after each dose; hold for SBP under 90 and notify.
Headache is expected and means the drug is working; acetaminophen may help.
Contraindicated within 24-48 hours of PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) - severe hypotension.
Store tablets in the original dark glass bottle; replace every 6 months; a tingle under the tongue means it is active.
Remove the old patch before applying a new one; wear gloves to avoid absorbing the drug.

uses: Edema from heart failure, liver, or kidney disease
quickTip: Potent diuretic that wastes potassium - watch K+ closely, and give IV slowly (no faster than 20 mg/min) to prevent ototoxicity.
administration: Oral in the morning (second dose no later than mid-afternoon) to avoid nocturia. IV push over 1-2 minutes; large doses by infusion.
mechanism: Blocks sodium and chloride reabsorption in the loop of Henle, so large amounts of water follow salt out in the urine.
simplified: Pulls the plug on the body's extra water.
nursing: Monitor potassium, sodium, BP, and daily weight; report a gain of 2 lb in a day or 5 lb in a week.
Hold for SBP under 90 or K+ under 3.5 and notify the provider.
Teach potassium-rich foods (bananas, oranges, potatoes) or give supplements as ordered.
Hypokalemia increases digoxin toxicity risk - check both when co-prescribed.
Sulfa allergy is a relative contraindication; rise slowly to prevent falls.

quickTip: First-line for hypertension but loses potassium and raises glucose, uric acid, and calcium - ask about gout and diabetes.
administration: Once daily in the morning with food to reduce nocturia and GI upset.
mechanism: Blocks sodium reabsorption in the distal tubule so the kidney excretes more salt and water, gently lowering blood volume.
simplified: A slow leak that eases pressure in the pipes.
nursing: Monitor potassium, sodium, glucose, uric acid, and BP.
Hold for K+ under 3.5 or SBP under 90 and notify.
Teach sunscreen and protective clothing; the drug increases sun sensitivity.
Not effective once GFR falls below about 30 mL/min - loop diuretics are used instead.
Sulfa-based - screen for sulfonamide allergy.

quickTip: The opposite potassium problem - it RETAINS potassium, so avoid salt substitutes and watch for hyperkalemia, especially with ACE inhibitors or ARBs.
administration: Once daily with food to improve absorption; take in the morning. Full diuretic effect takes 2-3 days.
mechanism: Blocks aldosterone in the collecting duct, so the kidney dumps sodium and water but holds onto potassium.
simplified: Lets water out while keeping potassium in.
nursing: Monitor potassium closely; hold and notify for K+ above 5.0.
Teach to avoid potassium-rich foods, potassium supplements, and salt substitutes.
Report muscle weakness, palpitations, or irregular pulse - signs of high potassium.
Breast tenderness or enlargement in men is reversible after stopping.
Weak diuretic alone; often paired with a loop or thiazide diuretic.

quickTip: Toxic to lungs, liver, thyroid, and eyes - baseline and periodic PFTs, LFTs, TFTs, and eye exams. Very long half-life means effects linger for weeks.
administration: Oral with meals for consistent absorption. IV through a central line when possible, using an in-line filter; monitor for hypotension during loading.
mechanism: Prolongs the heart's repolarization phase by blocking potassium channels, which lengthens the refractory period and stops re-entry rhythms.
simplified: Stretches out each heartbeat so the rhythm cannot race.
nursing: Continuous ECG during IV use; hold for HR under 60, new heart block, or QT prolongation.
Report new cough, dyspnea, or chest pain immediately - possible pulmonary toxicity.
Teach sunscreen and protective clothing; skin may turn blue-gray with long-term use.
Raises digoxin and warfarin levels - those doses usually need to be reduced.
Avoid grapefruit juice; report vision changes, tremor, or weight changes (thyroid).

quickTip: Unexplained muscle pain or weakness plus dark urine means possible rhabdomyolysis - stop the drug and check CK. Monitor liver enzymes.
administration: Once daily at any time (atorvastatin's long half-life does not require bedtime dosing). Avoid large amounts of grapefruit juice.
mechanism: Blocks the liver enzyme that makes cholesterol, so the liver pulls more LDL out of the blood to compensate.
simplified: Shuts down the liver's cholesterol factory.
nursing: Baseline and periodic LFTs; hold and notify for muscle pain, weakness, or dark urine.
Contraindicated in pregnancy, breastfeeding, and active liver disease.
Teach to limit alcohol and report yellow skin or eyes.
Lifestyle changes (diet, exercise) continue alongside the drug.
Recheck lipid panel in 4-12 weeks after starting or changing dose.

quickTip: Monitor PT/INR - therapeutic INR is usually 2-3 (2.5-3.5 for mechanical valves). Antidote is vitamin K (phytonadione). Takes 3-5 days to reach full effect.
administration: Once daily at the same time, usually in the evening, so the day's INR result can adjust the dose. Overlap with heparin until INR is therapeutic.
mechanism: Blocks vitamin K recycling in the liver, so the clotting factors that depend on it (II, VII, IX, X) are made in inactive form.
simplified: Starves the liver of the vitamin it needs to build clots.
nursing: Check INR before dosing; hold and notify if above target range or if bleeding is present.
Keep vitamin K intake CONSISTENT (leafy greens) - do not eliminate, just avoid big swings.
Many drug interactions: antibiotics, amiodarone, and NSAIDs raise bleeding risk; report new prescriptions.
Teach soft toothbrush, electric razor, and reporting black stools, blood in urine, or unusual bruising.
Contraindicated in pregnancy; heparin or LMWH is used instead.

uses: Clot prevention in dialysis and surgery
quickTip: Monitor aPTT - therapeutic is 1.5-2.5 times control (about 60-80 seconds). Antidote is protamine sulfate. Watch platelets for HIT.
administration: Subcutaneous in the abdomen, 2 inches from the umbilicus, 90-degree angle, no aspiration, no massage. IV infusion by weight-based protocol on a pump; always double-check dose with a second nurse.
mechanism: Boosts antithrombin III, which quickly inactivates thrombin and factor Xa so new clots cannot form and existing ones cannot grow.
simplified: Supercharges the body's own clot-stopper.
nursing: Monitor aPTT every 6 hours during IV therapy until stable; check platelets every 2-3 days.
Platelet drop over 50% or below 100,000 suggests HIT - stop heparin and notify immediately.
Protamine sulfate reverses it; keep it available on the unit.
Rotate abdominal SubQ sites; do not aspirate or rub.
Does not cross the placenta - safe anticoagulant choice in pregnancy.

quickTip: Do NOT expel the air bubble from the prefilled syringe - it seals the dose. No routine aPTT needed; check platelets and renal function.
administration: Deep subcutaneous in the abdominal 'love handles', 2 inches from the umbilicus, 90-degree angle, air bubble left in, no aspiration or massage. Alternate sides.
mechanism: A smaller form of heparin that mainly inactivates factor Xa, giving a predictable effect with once- or twice-daily injections.
simplified: Heparin's precise little cousin - no drip, no aPTT.
nursing: Monitor CBC and platelets; anti-Xa levels only in pregnancy, obesity, or renal impairment.
Reduce dose or avoid when creatinine clearance is under 30 mL/min.
Epidural or spinal catheters increase risk of spinal hematoma - report back pain or leg weakness.
Protamine partially reverses it.
Teach self-injection technique and bleeding precautions for home use.

quickTip: After a coronary stent it must NOT be stopped without cardiology approval - stent thrombosis can be fatal. Hold 5-7 days before elective surgery only when instructed.
administration: Once daily with or without food; often paired with low-dose aspirin (dual antiplatelet therapy).
mechanism: A prodrug the liver activates; it permanently blocks the ADP receptor on platelets so they cannot clump together for their lifespan.
simplified: Makes platelets too slippery to stick together.
nursing: Monitor for bleeding and bruising; check CBC and platelets.
Omeprazole and esomeprazole reduce activation - pantoprazole is preferred if a PPI is needed.
Some patients are poor metabolizers (CYP2C19) and get little effect; genetic testing may be ordered.
Teach to report black stools, blood in urine, or purple skin spots.
Carry a card or bracelet stating antiplatelet therapy and stent date.

quickTip: Never give to children or teens with viral illness - Reye syndrome. Tinnitus is the early sign of salicylate toxicity.
administration: Chew non-enteric tablets during suspected MI for fastest effect. Otherwise take with food or a full glass of water; do not crush enteric-coated tablets.
mechanism: Permanently blocks the COX-1 enzyme in platelets so they cannot make thromboxane, the signal that makes them clump.
simplified: Switches off the platelet's stick-together signal for its whole life.
nursing: Hold 7 days before elective surgery only when ordered - platelet effect lasts the platelet's lifetime.
Assess for ulcer history, bleeding disorders, and asthma before starting.
Teach to report ringing in the ears, black stools, or coffee-ground vomit.
Avoid combining with other NSAIDs or alcohol; ibuprofen can block aspirin's heart benefit.
Low dose (81 mg) is used for cardiac protection; higher doses are for pain and fever.

quickTip: Ischemic stroke window is within 3 hours of symptom onset (up to 4.5 hours in selected patients). Rule out hemorrhage with a CT scan first - the drug dissolves ALL clots.
administration: IV bolus followed by infusion on a dedicated line; stroke dose is weight-based (0.9 mg/kg, max 90 mg) with 10% given as a bolus over 1 minute.
mechanism: Converts plasminogen into plasmin, the enzyme that breaks fibrin strands apart and dissolves the clot that is already formed.
simplified: Sends in the demolition crew to break up an existing clot.
nursing: Screen for contraindications: recent surgery, trauma, bleeding, hemorrhagic stroke, uncontrolled BP above 185/110.
Insert all IV lines and draw labs BEFORE starting; avoid injections, IM shots, and venipuncture for 24 hours.
Neuro checks and vital signs every 15 minutes during infusion and for the first 2 hours after.
Sudden headache, vomiting, or drop in level of consciousness - stop the infusion and call the provider (possible bleed).
Hold anticoagulants and antiplatelets for 24 hours after stroke dosing until a repeat CT is clear.

uses: Prevention of potassium loss with diuretics
quickTip: NEVER give IV push - it stops the heart. IV must be diluted and infused by pump, typically no faster than 10 mEq/hour on a regular unit.
administration: Oral with a full glass of water and food; do not crush extended-release tablets. Liquid or powder must be diluted. IV only via pump, ideally through a central line at higher concentrations.
mechanism: Directly replaces potassium, the main ion inside cells that sets the resting electrical charge of heart and muscle tissue.
simplified: Refills the battery that keeps the heart's rhythm steady.
nursing: Check serum potassium and urine output before giving; hold if K+ above 5.0 or urine output under 30 mL/hr.
Confirm adequate renal function - the kidneys must be able to excrete the extra potassium.
Continuous ECG for IV infusions above 10 mEq/hr; watch for peaked T waves.
Assess IV site frequently - potassium is very irritating; slow or stop for burning.
Teach to report muscle weakness, palpitations, or numbness, and to sit upright for 30 minutes after oral doses.
